P.label: What is a MF
P.title: What a mutual fund is and how it works
P.short: Mutual fund: pooled trust run by professionals
P.law: A mutual fund is a trust that pools the savings of numerous investors who share a common financial goal, through the issue of units, and invests them in capital market instruments (shares, debentures, bonds) and money market instruments (CPs, CDs, T-Bills). The net income and capital appreciation are shared among unit holders in proportion to the units they own. The fund house charges fees based on the value of the assets it manages.
notes: Investor = part owner of all the fund's assets and liabilities.
Who can invest: anyone with an investible surplus of as little as a few thousand rupees, by buying units of a scheme with a defined objective.

Stocks or MF? A well-diversified portfolio needs 15–20 stocks; with ₹5,000 that is impractical alone but possible through a fund. SIP of ₹1,000 a month builds discipline. Picking stocks needs time, skill and inclination; otherwise hand the money to professional managers. MFs suit risk-averse investors.
Tax point in the SM: mutual funds do not pay capital gains tax when they sell a stock; an individual churning a portfolio does.
P.mem: Pool → Professionals → Proportionate share.

P.label: Establishing a MF
P.title: Establishment of a mutual fund: sponsor, trust, AMC, custodian
P.short: Sponsor → trustees → AMC → custodian (SEBI)
P.law: A mutual fund must be registered with SEBI before it collects money from the public. It is established by a sponsor (a body corporate in financial services for at least 5 years, financially sound and a fit party), as a trust under the Indian Trusts Act (trust deed registered under the Registration Act, 1908, containing the Third Schedule clauses) or a trustee company. An SEBI-approved Asset Management Company (minimum net worth ₹100 crore per the SM; sponsor contributes at least 40% of it) manages the schemes. A SEBI-registered custodian, independent of the sponsor and AMC, holds the securities.
notes: Sponsor is like a promoter: provides initial capital and appoints the trustees; executes the trust deed in favour of the trustees.
Trustees hold the property of the fund in trust for the unit holders. At least two-thirds of the trustee board/trustee company directors must be independent of the sponsor.
AMC board: at least 50% independent directors. Its appointment can be terminated by a majority of trustees or by 75% of the unit holders of the scheme.
AMC fees: investment management and advisory fees within the prescribed ceiling, plus reimbursement of scheme operating expenses.
Custodian: for dematerialised securities the job is done through a Depository Participant.
This is SM TYK Theory Q1 — a full 4–5 mark answer lists sponsor, trust, AMC (net worth, 40%, independence, termination), custodian.
P.mem: S-T-A-C: Sponsor (5 yrs, 40%) · Trust (⅔ independent) · AMC (₹100 cr per SM, 50% independent, removable by 75% unit holders) · Custodian (independent).

P.label: Open/close/interval
P.title: Functional classification: open-ended, close-ended and interval funds
P.short: Open-ended vs close-ended vs interval
P.law: Open-ended: enter and exit any time; capital unlimited; redemption period indefinite. Close-ended: invest at the NFO or buy on the stock exchange after listing; limited life after which the corpus is liquidated; exit by selling on the exchange, at expiry, or in a repurchase period. Interval: a mix — open for purchase and redemption only at pre-specified intervals at NAV-based prices.
notes: Interval vs close-ended: interval funds need not be listed (in-built redemption window), can issue fresh units during the interval at NAV-based prices, and have no defined maturity.
Liquidity: open-ended funds give it through direct sale/repurchase by the fund; close-ended funds through listing on the exchange.
Capital Protection Oriented Funds, Real Estate MFs and FMPs are required to be close-ended (see special funds, types of schemes).

P.label: Equity & debt funds
P.title: Portfolio classification: equity funds, debt funds and the four bond-fund risks
P.short: Equity (growth/aggressive/income) and debt funds
P.law: Equity funds: (a) Growth — long-term capital appreciation; (b) Aggressive — super-normal returns from start-ups, IPOs, speculative shares; (c) Income — present income from safe high-dividend stocks and high-yield money market instruments. Debt funds: (a) Bond funds — fixed income securities; less volatile than equity funds, but carry interest rate, credit, prepayment and reinvestment risk; (b) Gilt funds — T-Bills and dated securities of Central and State Governments.
notes: Interest rate risk: bond value moves inversely to interest rates (YTM).
Credit risk: issuer defaults on interest or principal; higher for lower-rated issuers.
Prepayment risk: issuer calls callable bonds early when rates fall and refinances cheaper.
Reinvestment risk: maturity proceeds reinvested at lower rates when rates fall; favourable when rates rise.
Portfolio classification has three heads: equity, debt and special funds.
P.mem: Bond-fund risks: I-C-P-R (Interest, Credit, Prepayment, Reinvestment).

P.label: Gilt fund & duration
P.title: Gilt fund: NAV from bond holdings and churning to change duration
P.short: Lengthen duration if rates fall, shorten if rates rise
P.law: A fund investing in dated Government securities is a gilt fund. NAV per unit = Σ(face value × purchase/market price ÷ 100) ÷ units. To manage interest rate risk the manager churns the portfolio: when rates are expected to fall, increase average duration (sell the shortest bond, buy the longest) to gain more on price; when rates are expected to rise, reduce average duration (sell the longest, buy a shorter one).
notes: Average duration (simple average, per ICAI's note) = Σ durations ÷ number of bonds; revised = (Σ − duration sold + duration bought) ÷ n.
RTP Nov 2026 / MTP May 2026: average 7.85 → 9.75 years (rates −25 bp: sell GOI 2026, buy GOI 2052) and → 6.55 years (rates +75 bp: sell GOI 2052, buy GOI 2030).
ICAI does not buy the shortest bond (GOI 2026) in the rising-rate case: its maturity is very short and a 75 bp move is comparatively large.
Links to interest rate risk under debt funds.
P.mem: Rates down → duration up. Rates up → duration down.

P.label: Special funds
P.title: Special funds: index, international, offshore, sector, money market, FoF, capital protection, gold, quant
P.short: Index, FoF, capital protection, gold, quant etc.
P.law: Index fund: invests in index stocks in the same weights; passively managed, low cost. International fund: raises money in India, invests globally. Offshore fund: located outside India, raises money globally to invest in India. Sector fund: entire fund in one sector. Money market fund: preservation of capital, liquidity, moderate income from CPs, CDs, T-Bills. Fund of Funds: invests in units of other MF schemes. Capital Protection Oriented Fund: protection comes from the portfolio structure, not from any bank guarantee or insurance; SEBI requires it to be close-ended, listed and its portfolio structure rated. Gold fund: tracks gold, usually an ETF. Quant fund: data-driven, rule-based model decides stock, quantity and timing.
notes: International vs offshore: the classic pair — direction of money flow is reversed.
Capital protection ≠ capital guaranteed: most assets in highly rated debt for safety, the rest in equity for appreciation.

Quant fund pros: removes human bias and subjectivity, consistent strategy across market conditions, usually lower expense ratio (passive-like). Cons: models are tested on historical data, which cannot be used blindly.
Quant vs index fund manager: the index manager simply follows the index; the quant manager designs and monitors models and decides on their output. There is still some human intervention.
Money market funds are less vulnerable to interest rate changes and less volatile than long-dated bond funds.
P.mem: International = India → world. Offshore = world → India.

P.label: Types of schemes
P.title: Types of schemes: balanced, diversified equity, ELSS, sector, thematic, arbitrage, cash, FMP
P.short: Balanced, flexicap/multicap, ELSS, FMP, arbitrage
P.law: Balanced: strategic mix of debt (stability) and equity (growth). Diversified equity: Flexicap — any proportion across market caps; Multicap — at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps, rest at discretion; Contra — out-of-favour, undervalued companies; Index; Dividend yield — high dividend yield stocks. ELSS: tax saving under s.80C with a 3-year lock-in. Sector and thematic funds. Arbitrage: profits from spot–futures price differences. Cash fund: open-ended liquid scheme. FMP: close-ended debt fund whose investments mature with the fund, so free from interest rate risk but carries credit risk.
notes: Sector funds ride industry cycles: good returns if timing is right, but riskier than diversified funds; only a limited portion of a portfolio and not for first-time investors. Example: Real Estate MFs — must be close-ended and listed.
Thematic funds have a broader outlook than sector funds (multi-sector, international, commodity themes); the market may take long to recognise the theme.
Dividend yield funds: medium risk; prices less volatile than growth stocks, but not always resilient in short corrections.
FMPs: bought in the NFO, listed but thinly traded, so illiquid; most have 3-year tenure (indexation); some money goes into AA and lower-rated paper for higher coupons.
ELSS through SIP avoids a year-end lump sum and gives rupee-cost averaging.
Hedge funds and ETFs have their own entries: hedge fund, ETFs.
P.upd: The SM's line that most FMPs have a 3-year tenure 'to take the benefit of indexation' reflects the tax law when it was written. The tax treatment of debt-fund gains has changed since; AFM does not test tax, so do not quote indexation as current.
P.mem: Multicap = 25-25-25 + 25 free. Flexicap = 100% free.

P.label: Growth vs dividend
P.title: Income options: growth, dividend payout, dividend reinvestment (and bonus plans)
P.short: Growth vs payout vs reinvestment option
P.law: Growth / cumulative option: no intermittent income; returns accumulate and are received on withdrawal as capital gain. Dividend option: the scheme declares dividends monthly/quarterly/half-yearly/annually. Payout — dividend is paid and the NAV falls by the dividend and statutory levies. Reinvestment — dividend is reinvested at the ex-dividend NAV, so the investor gets additional units.
notes: Reinvestment units = (units held × face value × dividend %) ÷ ex-dividend NAV. Dividend % is on face value (₹10), not on NAV.
Bonus plan: free units in the bonus ratio (1:5 means 1 new for every 5 held); NAV adjusts down; no cash.
Worked in plan-wise effective yield.

P.label: Direct plans
P.title: Direct plans (SEBI, 1 January 2013) and ownership classification
P.short: Direct plan: no distribution cost, higher NAV
P.law: SEBI introduced direct plans from 1 January 2013. In a direct plan the AMC does not charge distribution expenses, trail fees or transaction charges, so its NAV is generally higher than the regular plan and it has performed better to the extent of the lower fees. Ownership classification: public sector MFs (sponsored by a public sector company/bank), private sector MFs, and foreign MFs (sponsored by a foreign company operating from India, raising and investing funds in India).
notes: Before 2013, direct investments were tracked in a regular plan with a single NAV.
Link: trail commission is exactly what a direct plan saves.

P.label: ETFs
P.title: Exchange Traded Funds
P.short: ETF: index fund that trades like a share
P.law: ETFs are hybrids combining the features of listed stocks and index funds. They are listed, priced in line with the underlying index, and can be bought or sold any time during market hours at real-time prices close to NAV (unlike open-ended schemes, priced at end-of-day NAV). Authorised participants act as market makers. Types: index, commodity, bond and currency ETFs.
notes: Why attractive: low cost, tax efficiency, stock-like features, no paperwork (order through a broker).
Combines the valuation feature of a mutual fund (redeemable at NAV) with the tradability of a closed-end fund (trades through the day, possibly away from NAV).
Bond ETFs thrive in recessions as money moves from stocks to bonds; their performance can signal economic conditions.
Currency ETFs: total-return products giving FX spot change, local institutional interest rates and a collateral yield.
P.mem: ETF = Index fund + Share.

P.label: Hedge fund & fees
P.title: Hedge funds and the high-water-mark incentive fee
P.short: Hedge fund fee: fixed fee + incentive above high-water mark
P.law:
A hedge fund is a lightly regulated private investment vehicle for selected clients. Unlike a mutual fund it discloses little publicly and charges a performance fee, taking a cut of profits above a benchmark while investors bear all losses. It uses leverage, long/short and derivative positions to maximise return (despite the name, not to reduce risk).

Fee computation: Fixed fee = % × opening assets. Incentive fee = % × (closing value − highest value achieved since inception), only if positive.
notes: Steps: (1) fixed fee on current assets; (2) new value = assets × (1 + return); (3) excess over the high-water mark; (4) incentive % × excess, nil if not above the mark; (5) total.
SM TYK (ANP Plan): assets ₹20 crore, fixed 0.10%, incentive 2% above max value ₹21 crore. 29% → 2 lakh + 9.60 lakh = ₹11.60 lakh; 4.5% → value ₹20.90 crore, below 21 → ₹2 lakh only; −1.8% → ₹2 lakh.
Trap: computing the incentive on the year's gain (₹20 crore base) instead of the excess over the high-water mark (₹21 crore).
P.mem: Incentive only above the high-water mark.

P.label: Advantages
P.title: Advantages of mutual funds
P.short: 12 advantages: professional management to convenience
P.law: (a) Professional management; (b) Diversification reduces concentration risk; (c) Convenient administration (demat, no transfer risk); (d) Higher returns over the medium-long term; (e) Low cost of management — SEBI cap of 2.50% for equity funds, excess borne by the AMC; (f) Liquidity; (g) Transparency — portfolio disclosure at least half-yearly, daily NAV for open-ended funds; (h) Other benefits — SIP, SWP, switches (except ELSS for 3 years); (i) Highly regulated by SEBI; (j) Economies of scale; (k) Flexibility; (l) Convenience through digital platforms.
notes: This is SM TYK Theory Q2. ICAI's answer: 'Please refer paragraph 4' — i.e. list the heads with one line each.
Boom-period returns (IT, infrastructure) should not be treated as regular; look at long-run averages.
Pair with drawbacks for 'advantages and disadvantages' questions.
P.upd: The 2.50% expense cap is the SM's figure. SEBI's TER limits have been revised since; quote the SM figure in the exam.
P.mem: PD-CHL-LTO-HEFC: Professional, Diversification, Convenient admin, Higher returns, Low cost, Liquidity, Transparency, Other benefits, Highly regulated, Economies of scale, Flexibility, Convenience.

P.label: Drawbacks
P.title: Drawbacks of mutual funds
P.short: No guarantee, diversification caps returns, selection, cost
P.law: (a) No guarantee of return: not every scheme beats its benchmark; the fund's gain differs from each investor's because of different entry and exit points; principal can be lost in a crash (2008, Covid-19 2020), though rarely over the long term. (b) Diversification minimises risk but does not maximise return — a stock that doubles does not double the fund. (c) Selecting the right fund is harder than selecting a share; past performance cannot predict the future. (d) Cost: annual recurring fees and exit loads, and the AMC's fee is not related to performance.
notes: MFs 'tend to do neither exceptionally well nor exceptionally poorly'.
P.mem: No-Div-Sel-Cost.

P.label: NAV
P.title: Net Asset Value: computing NAV per unit
P.short: NAV = (assets − liabilities) ÷ units outstanding
P.law:
NAV per unit = Net assets of the scheme ÷ Number of units outstanding.

Net assets = Market value of investments + Receivables + Other accrued income + Other assets − Accrued expenses − Other payables − Other liabilities.

NAV is the market value of total assets less liabilities, on a per-unit basis; it changes daily.
notes: Valuation rules used in ICAI answers: listed shares at market price; shares bought at an index level can be scaled by the index movement (cost × present index ÷ base index); listed bonds at their NAV-date value; unlisted bonds at cost less any diminution; cash at book; accrued dividend and income added; amounts payable on shares and accrued expenses deducted.
New subscription: new units issued = cheque ÷ current NAV. Buying shares with it only changes the asset mix; NAV is unchanged on day 1 (the rest sits as cash).
Next-day NAV = revalued holdings (with the new shares) + cash ÷ new total units.
Cash build-up: opening cash (amount raised − amount invested) + dividends + interest received − expenses paid − distributions.
After a dividend, NAV falls by the dividend per unit (total distribution leaves the fund).

SM TYKs: Cinderella MF ₹41.57; L/M/N/P Ltd ₹78.84 → 6,38,053 units → ₹82.26; Fair Return MF ₹119.05 → 8,42,000 units → ₹122.075; issue of 10 lakh units ₹11.55 → ₹10.75 after ₹0.80 dividend; regular income scheme ₹271.30.
P.mem: Assets at market − liabilities ÷ units.

P.label: Entry & exit load
P.title: Entry load, exit load, public offer price and redemption price
P.short: Front-end / back-end load and offer / redemption price
P.law:
Entry (front-end) load is added to NAV at purchase, so fewer units are allotted. Exit (back-end) load is deducted from NAV at redemption or switch; it goes into the scheme's pool, not to the AMC. No-load funds have neither. At present no scheme charges an entry load, and most have no exit load after a stipulated holding period.

ICAI formulae: Public Offer Price = NAV ÷ (1 − Front-end load); Redemption Price = NAV ÷ (1 + Back-end load). Alternative: load = (POP − NAV) ÷ NAV; exit load = (NAV − redemption price) ÷ NAV.
notes: SM TYK (ELSS): NAV ₹10, POP ₹10.204, redemption ₹9.80 → front-end load 2% (or 2.04% by the alternative), back-end load 2.04% (or 2%). ICAI accepts both methods.
In dividend-equalisation sums ICAI simply takes issue price = NAV + load % × NAV and repurchase price = NAV − load % × NAV, then adds the equalisation amount (see dividend equalisation).

Loads in return sums: entry load raises the cost per unit (₹22.01 + ₹0.05 entry load per unit); exit load cuts redemption value (1% of ₹3,75,000). Return is on the amount actually paid. Real return = (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1 (PYQ Sep 2025 Q5(b): 27.71% → 22.21%).
P.mem: Front: divide by (1 − f). Back: divide by (1 + b).

P.label: Required MF return
P.title: Return a fund must earn to cover initial and recurring expenses
P.short: r₂ = r₁ ÷ (1 − initial exp.) + recurring exp.
P.law:
r2 = [1 ÷ (1 − Initial expenses)] × r1 + Recurring expenses

where r1 = return the investor can earn on his own and r2 = return the scheme must earn so that the investor still gets r1.
notes: Why: initial expenses mean only (1 − i) of each rupee is invested, so the invested part must earn r1/(1 − i); recurring expenses are charged every year on top.
SM Example: r1 10%, initial 6%, recurring 2% → 0.10/0.94 + 0.02 = 12.64%.
SM TYK: r1 16%, initial 5.5%, recurring 1.5% → 0.16/0.945 + 0.015 = 18.43%.
Trap: adding initial expenses as a % (10 + 6 + 2) or dividing recurring expenses too.
P.mem: Gross up for initial, add on recurring.

P.label: Trail commission
P.title: Trail commission
P.short: Annual fee to the distributor on assets
P.law: Trail commission is the amount a mutual fund investor pays to his advisor/distributor each year while the money stays invested, to give the advisor an incentive to review holdings and advise. Usually 0.30%–0.75% of the value of the investment, computed on the daily average AUM of the distributor and paid monthly. It is separate from any upfront commission the fund company pays from its own pocket.
notes: Direct plans carry no trail commission — see direct plans.

P.label: Expense ratio
P.title: Expense ratio (TER / MER)
P.short: % of assets spent to run the fund
P.law: The expense ratio is the percentage of the assets spent to run a mutual fund: management and advisory fees, travel, audit, custodian, registrar and consultancy fees. It does not include brokerage on trading the portfolio. Also called the Management Expense Ratio (MER) or Total Expense Ratio (TER). It can be as high as 2–3%, which seriously undermines performance.
notes: SM: SEBI's maximum for equity funds is 2.50%; any extra cost is borne by the AMC (see advantages).
A financial measure in quantitative evaluation.
P.mem: TER excludes brokerage.

P.label: Side pocketing
P.title: Side pocketing
P.short: Ring-fencing stressed assets from the main portfolio
P.law: Side pocketing separates risky or doubtful (stressed, illiquid) assets from the other investments and cash. When an asset's rating falls, the fund shifts it into a side pocket, so the NAV of the main fund reflects only the liquid assets and existing holders benefit from them. Money linked to the stressed asset stays locked until the fund recovers it, avoiding distress selling.
notes: Benefits long-term holders of the main fund; keeps liquidity intact despite frequent allotments and redemptions.
Common internationally, but has also been misused to deny investors genuine returns.
India: the IL&FS default (liquidity crisis) drove the debate; funds wrote off IL&FS exposure and gave low to negative returns.
P.mem: Bad apple in a side box; NAV shows the good apples.

P.label: Tracking error
P.title: Tracking error
P.short: TE = standard deviation of return differences
P.law:
Tracking error is the divergence of a fund's return from the return of the benchmark it follows.

TE = √[ Σ(d − d̄)² ÷ (n − 1) ], where d = differential return (fund − benchmark), d̄ = average differential return, n = number of observations.
notes: Higher TE = higher risk profile; outperforming or underperforming both show the manager is not tracking properly. To replicate an index, TE should be near zero.
Causes: transaction cost, fees charged by AMCs, fund expenses, cash holdings, sampling bias.
Computed on benchmark returns versus quarterly or monthly average NAVs.
A passive fund manager's main job is minimum TE — see fund managers.
Trap: dividing by n instead of n − 1 (it is a sample standard deviation).
P.mem: TE = SD of (fund − index).

P.label: Dividend equalisation
P.title: Dividend equalisation on issue and repurchase of units
P.short: Issue/repurchase price includes income per unit to date
P.law:
When units are issued or repurchased in the middle of a period, the price is adjusted for dividend equalisation: the incoming investor pays, and the outgoing investor receives, the undistributed income per unit accumulated so far. This keeps income per unit the same for old and new unit holders.

Issue price = NAV + entry load + income per unit to date. Repurchase price = NAV − exit load + income per unit to date.
notes: Steps (SM TYK, 300 lakh units): (1) income per unit each month = month's income ÷ units outstanding; (2) add equalisation collected on issue, deduct equalisation paid on repurchase; (3) dividend = % × available income; (4) closing NAV = opening net assets + appreciation + issue proceeds + income − repurchases − dividend, ÷ closing units.
Answers: income after distribution ₹30.8151 lakh; issue price ₹19.2015; repurchase price ₹18.564; NAV on 30 June ₹20.2670.
Load is on the opening NAV given in the question — ICAI does not grow the NAV month by month.
P.mem: New investor buys his share of income already earned.

P.label: Holding period return
P.title: Return on a mutual fund with income and capital-gain distributions
P.short: r = (NAVₜ − NAVₜ₋₁ + Iₜ + Gₜ) ÷ NAVₜ₋₁
P.law:
r = [(NAVt − NAVt−1) + It + Gt] ÷ NAVt−1

I = income (dividend) distributed, G = capital-gain distribution, per unit. With reinvestment: extra units = total distributions ÷ reinvestment NAV; return = (closing units × closing NAV − original cost) ÷ original cost.
notes: Monthly return × 12 = annual (simple) — SM TYK 0.6375% p.m. = 7.65% p.a.
Back-solve NAV: given annual 15% → monthly 1.25%; 0.0125 = (NAVt − 65.78 + 0.50 + 0.32) ÷ 65.78 → NAVt = ₹65.78 (no change: distributions exactly equal the month's return).
Payout vs reinvest: compare the two returns and advise the higher (SM TYK: 23.43% vs 24.85% → reinvest). Reinvestment wins when reinvestment NAV is below closing NAV.
P.mem: Change in NAV + what was paid out, over what you paid.

P.label: Effective yield p.a.
P.title: Effective (annualised) yield on MF investments, and back-solving from it
P.short: Yield = (NAV gain + dividends) ÷ cost × 365 ÷ days
P.law:
Effective yield p.a. = [(Closing value − Investment) + Dividends received] ÷ Investment × 365 ÷ Days held × 100, where units = investment ÷ entry NAV and closing value = units × closing NAV.

Reverse: Days held = Yield % (for the period) × 365 ÷ Effective yield p.a.; date of investment = valuation date − days.
notes: SM TYK Mr Y (reverse): units 19,417.48 / 39,603.96 / 20,000; total NAV ₹7,99,068.77; total yield ₹10,068.77 (1.2586%); days 95 / 31 / 68 → invested 27.12.17, 01.03.18, 23.01.18 (alternatively one day earlier).

Mr X NAV puzzle: annualised yield × months/12 gives the period yield; market value = cost × (1 + yield); NAV after a payout dividend = (value − dividend) ÷ units; reinvested units = dividend ÷ NAV. Answers ₹20.50, ₹25.95, ₹26.75.
Count days exactly (both ICAI answers count from the entry date to the valuation date, excluding the first day).

P.label: Plan-wise yield
P.title: Comparing dividend-reinvestment, bonus and growth plans
P.short: Units trail for reinvest/bonus plans, then annual return
P.law: Build a units table for each plan to the redemption date: dividend reinvestment — new units = units held × face value × dividend % ÷ ex-dividend NAV on that date; bonus — new units = units held × bonus ratio; growth — units unchanged. Redemption value = closing units × closing NAV, less STT and tax where given. Annual return = Net gain ÷ Investment × 12 ÷ months held (or IRR, which ICAI accepts as the alternative).
notes: Short-term capital gain only on units acquired within the short-term period (in the SM's Sun Moon question, the reinvestment/bonus units of 24.3.2009) — earlier units are long-term and exempt by the question's assumption.
SM TYK Sun Moon MF (STT 0.2%, STCG 10%): Charu (A, reinvest) net gain ₹6,98,969.69 → 67.64% p.a.; Anand (B, bonus) ₹7,57,791.50 → 73.33%; Bacchan (C, growth) ₹7,19,058.60 → 69.59% (124 months).
ICAI note: under the 5th proviso to s.48 of the Income-tax Act, STT is not deductible in computing capital gains — so the sale price for STCG can be taken without deducting STT.

Reverse (RTP May 2023, Corpus AMC): from average profit or yield, find closing value → closing units; strip reinvested units backwards (new units = closing units × dividend ÷ (NAV + dividend)) or bonus units (× 5/6, × 4/5) to the original units; issue price = investment ÷ original units (₹46 and ₹50).

Back-solving the issue price is a repeat PYQ pattern (Dec 2021 old Q1(b) ₹49.78; May 2023 Q5(a) ₹54 and ₹80; Jan 2026 Q1(a) ₹95.87): total value = investment + average annual gain × years; units at the end = value ÷ closing NAV; remove each reinvestment (N + N × ₹10 × d% ÷ NAV = closing units) or bonus (× 4/5, × 5/7) going backwards; issue price = investment ÷ original units.
With loads (PYQ May 2026 Q3(b)): units = investment ÷ (NAV × 1.02); redemption at NAV × 0.99 — dividend plan 19.90% vs bonus plan 31.43%.
P.mem: Dividend % × face value, ÷ NAV for new units.

P.label: Fund-level rate of earning
P.title: Fund's month: cash, closing NAV and investor's rate of earning
P.short: Build cash and closing net assets, then return per unit
P.law: For a new fund over a period: opening cash = funds raised − initial expenses − portfolio bought; add sale proceeds and dividends; deduct purchases, expenses paid and distributions → closing cash. Closing net assets = closing cash + market value of portfolio − expenses in arrears. Closing NAV = net assets ÷ units. Investor's earning per unit = distributions received + (closing NAV − issue price).
notes: SM TYK ABC MF (April 2012): closing cash ₹0.80 lakh, net assets ₹198 lakh, NAV ₹9.90; earning = income ₹0.20 − loss ₹0.10 = ₹0.10 per unit → 1% a month → 12% p.a.
Distribution = % × realised earnings (capital gains on sale + dividends), not on unrealised appreciation.

PYQ Jan 2026 Q6(a) (Stork Capital): an underwriter takes up the whole 200 lakh units (commission 2%) even though only 180 lakh were subscribed; management expenses chargeable = lower of actual and the SEBI cap (0.50% of average funds invested); uncollected dividend is a receivable. NAV ₹11.46.

P.label: Closed-end premium/discount
P.title: Closed-ended fund trading at a premium or discount to NAV
P.short: Market price = NAV × (1 ± premium/discount); GM return
P.law: Units of a close-ended fund trade on the exchange at a price that can be above (premium) or below (discount) NAV. Market price = NAV × (1 + premium %) or NAV × (1 − discount %). The investor's return comes from market prices, not NAV: geometric return per period = (closing price ÷ opening price)1/n − 1. The fund's own performance is the geometric growth in NAV = (closing NAV ÷ opening NAV)1/n − 1.
notes: PYQ May 2026 Q4(b): NAV 20 → 22.3 over 4 periods, ending at a 4% premium (price ₹23.192). Investor's GM return 3.771% per period; NAV growth 2.76%. The investor did better because the discount at entry (0%) turned into a premium at exit.
Interpretation: return > NAV growth means the market price rose more than NAV (discount narrowed or premium widened).
See close-ended funds and ETFs (which trade close to NAV).
P.mem: Investor earns the price; the fund earns the NAV.

P.label: Quantitative evaluation
P.title: Evaluating a mutual fund: quantitative parameters (Sharpe, Treynor, Sortino, alpha)
P.short: Risk-adjusted return, benchmark, peers, cycles, ratios
P.law: (1) Risk-adjusted returns — of two funds with the same return, choose the lower risk; (2) Benchmark returns — excess over the benchmark is alpha; (3) Comparison with peers of the same category; (4) Returns across economic and market cycles; (5) Financial measures: expense ratio; Sharpe ratio = (Rp − Rf) ÷ σp (total risk); Treynor ratio = (Rp − Rf) ÷ βp (systematic risk, β against the fund's benchmark); Sortino ratio — Sharpe with downside deviation instead of total σ.
notes: Evaluate at least every 6–12 months; give an equity fund 3–5 years. Daily evaluation is not advisable.
Past performance cannot guarantee future performance — that is why evaluation is continuous.
Jensen's alpha = R<sub>p</sub> − [R<sub>f</sub> + β(R<sub>m</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>)] (from Portfolio Management) is used in RTP/MTP fund-ranking sums.
Ranking sums: compute each ratio for every fund, rank, and comment that Sharpe suits an undiversified investor, Treynor a well-diversified one.
Add qualitative parameters for a complete answer.
β from correlation: β<sub>p</sub> = r × σ<sub>p</sub> ÷ σ<sub>m</sub> (RTP Dec 2021 five-portfolio ranking).
Risk per unit of return = σ ÷ expected return (RTP May 2024): choose the fund with the lower figure.

Reverse sums: σ = (Rp − Rf) ÷ Sharpe; β = (Rp − Rf) ÷ Treynor; correlation = β × σm ÷ σp; coefficient of determination = correlation² (PYQ Nov 2024 Q6(a)). From Jensen's alpha and Treynor, solve two equations for β and Rf (PYQ May 2023 Q5(b)).
P.mem: Sharpe = σ (total). Treynor = β (systematic). Sortino = downside σ.

P.label: Qualitative evaluation
P.title: Evaluating a mutual fund: qualitative parameters
P.short: Portfolio quality, fund manager, fund house
P.law: (1) Quality of portfolio — equity: blue-chip/large companies, diversification, style (growth, value, blend); debt: credit quality, average maturity, modified duration; investments must match the fund's objective; a lower portfolio turnover ratio is generally better. (2) Track record and competence of the fund manager — knowledge, ability, past performance. (3) Credibility of the fund house team — redemptions, dividend credits, information to investors.
notes: Pair with quantitative parameters: 'how would you evaluate a mutual fund?' wants both.
P.mem: Portfolio · Person · Place (fund house).

P.label: Expected NAV via beta
P.title: Expected NAV after a market move, using β derived from Sharpe and Treynor
P.short: β = σ × Sharpe ÷ Treynor; equity part moves β × market
P.law: (1) Split NAV into equity and cash elements. (2) Excess return = Sharpe × σ; β = Excess return ÷ Treynor. (3) Equity element changes by β × market change. (4) Cash element falls by the period's expenses. (5) Expected NAV = revised equity + remaining cash.
notes: SM TYK D and K Mutual Fund: D NAV ₹70.71 (99% equity → ₹70 equity, ₹0.71 cash), Sharpe 2, σ 11.25 → excess 22.50, Treynor 15 → β 1.50; K NAV ₹62.50 (96% → ₹60 + ₹2.50), Sharpe 3.3, σ 5 → 16.50 → β 1.10.
Market −5%: D equity −7.5% → ₹64.75; K −5.5% → ₹56.70. Cash less ₹3 ÷ 12 = ₹0.25: ₹0.46 and ₹2.25. Expected NAVs ₹65.21 and ₹58.95.
Trap: applying beta to the whole NAV, cash included.
P.mem: Sharpe × σ ÷ Treynor = β.

P.label: Role of fund manager
P.title: Role of fund managers: active vs passive, and other key roles
P.short: Alpha (active) / minimum TE (passive) + 4 other roles
P.law: In an actively managed fund the manager uses research, judgement and due diligence to outperform the market and generate positive alpha. In a passively managed fund the job is to match the index with minimum tracking error. Other key roles: (a) Compliances — SEBI/AMFI guidelines, reporting of expense ratio and redemptions, investor awareness, documents on time; (b) Constant monitoring of performance — entry/exit decisions; judged on growth above inflation and interest rates; (c) Creation and protection of wealth — no reckless risk; fundamental and technical analysis; (d) Control over work outsourced to third parties.
notes: Fund manager is the 'gatekeeper' of the fund, like a portfolio manager for an individual.
Link: tracking error.
P.mem: C-M-W-O: Compliances, Monitoring, Wealth, Outsourcing.

P.label: Role of FIIs
P.title: Role of Foreign Institutional Investors in mutual funds
P.short: FIIs: governance, competition, capital inflow
P.law: FIIs are large foreign groups with substantial investible funds, registered abroad, investing in other countries' equity markets, hedge funds, pension funds and mutual funds. They can buy units of domestic MFs directly from the issuer or through a registered stock broker on a recognised exchange, within limits notified by SEBI. Their role: (a) enhanced corporate governance (due diligence before investing); (b) improved competition in the market; (c) improved inflow of capital — employment and foreign exchange position.
notes: FIIs have strong research teams; they often fuel a bullish market for a short period, bringing strong foreign currency inflows at that time.
P.mem: G-C-C: Governance, Competition, Capital.

P.label: Constant ratio plan
P.title: Formula plans: constant ratio plan vs buy and hold
P.short: Rebalance to fixed equity:bond ratio on a trigger
P.law: Under a constant ratio plan the investor keeps a fixed ratio between the aggressive (equity) and conservative (bond) portfolios, rebalancing whenever the trigger is hit (in the SM question, whenever NAV rises or falls by 15%). On each trigger: total value = conservative + units × NAV; reset each side to its ratio share; buy units when equity has fallen, sell when it has risen.
notes: SM TYK Sunidhi: ₹2 lakh split 50:50, NAV ₹40 → 2,500 units. Rebalance at ₹25 (buy 750), ₹36 (sell 496.53), ₹38 (sell 72.46), ₹50 (sell 321.72). Ending value ₹2,40,647.55 vs buy-and-hold ₹2,60,000 (₹1,00,000 + 2,500 × ₹52).

How ICAI reads the 15% trigger: each month's NAV is compared with the previous month's NAV. 40→25 (−37.5%) buy; 25→36 (+44%) sell; 36→32 (−11%) no action; 32→38 (+18.75%) sell; 38→37, 37→42 (+13.5%), 42→43 no action; 43→50 (+16.3%) sell; 50→52 no action.
Formula plans are covered in detail in the Portfolio Management chapter.
P.mem: Fall → buy, rise → sell, back to the ratio.

P.label: SIP / STP / SWP
P.title: Systematic plans: SIP, STP, SWP and rupee-cost averaging
P.short: Fixed amount at fixed intervals; average cost = harmonic mean
P.law:
Beyond the SM: added for concept-based questions. Not part of ICAI's chapter text.

A Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) invests a fixed amount at regular intervals; a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) redeems a fixed amount at regular intervals; a Systematic Transfer Plan (STP) moves a fixed amount from one scheme (usually liquid/debt) to another (usually equity). Because a fixed amount buys more units when NAV is low and fewer when NAV is high, the average cost per unit is the harmonic mean of the NAVs, which is never more than their simple average — this is rupee-cost averaging.
notes: The SM mentions SIP for financial discipline (para 1.5), ELSS through SIP for 'averaging' (3.3) and SIP/SWP as advantages (4(h), 4(k)).
Average cost per unit = total amount invested ÷ total units bought.
Rupee-cost averaging reduces the risk of investing a lump sum at a market peak; it does not guarantee a profit in a market that keeps falling.
See the formula bank: SIP average cost.
P.mem: Same rupees → more units when cheap.

P.label: Jensen, M², IR
P.title: Advanced performance measures: Jensen's alpha, M², information ratio, R², turnover
P.short: Alpha over CAPM, M² at market risk, IR over benchmark
P.law:
Beyond the SM: added for concept-based questions. Not part of ICAI's chapter text.

Jensen's alpha = Rp − [Rf + β(Rm − Rf)]: return above what CAPM requires for the fund's β. M² (Modigliani) = Rf + Sharpep × σm: the fund's return if levered or de-levered to the market's risk, compared directly with Rm. Information ratio = (Rp − Rbenchmark) ÷ tracking error: active return per unit of active risk. R² = correlation²: the share of a fund's movement explained by the market. Portfolio turnover = lower of purchases and sales ÷ average net assets: how actively the portfolio is churned.
notes: Jensen's alpha is used in ICAI MF questions (PYQ May 2023 Q5(b), RTP Dec 2021 Q5) and in Portfolio Management.
M² ranks funds exactly like Sharpe, but in % terms you can compare with the market return.
Information ratio suits benchmarked active funds; it links tracking error to alpha.
A high R² with a high alpha is more trustworthy than a high alpha with a low R² (the benchmark may be wrong).
SM: a lower portfolio turnover ratio is generally better (qualitative parameters).
P.mem: Alpha = beat CAPM. M² = beat market at same risk. IR = beat index per unit of straying.

P.label: MF vocabulary
P.title: Operating vocabulary: NFO, AUM, AMFI, offer documents, switches, folios
P.short: NFO, AUM, AMFI, switch, folio, cut-off
P.law:
Beyond the SM: added for concept-based questions. Not part of ICAI's chapter text.

NFO (New Fund Offer): the first subscription period of a scheme, usually at face value. AUM (assets under management): total market value of assets a scheme or AMC manages. AMFI: the industry association that publishes NAVs (the SM says NAVs are published through AMFI). Offer document: the scheme's objective, asset allocation, loads and risks — it spells out the market-cap limits for each category (SM 3.2). Switch: redeeming from one scheme and investing in another of the same fund house; may attract exit load. Folio: the investor's account number with an AMC. Cut-off time: applications received before it get that day's NAV; after it, the next day's NAV — which is why investors cannot buy at a NAV already known (no 'late trading').
notes: Exit load applies on switches too (SM 6.2: exit load is charged at redemption 'or transferring an investment between schemes').
ELSS restricts switch-out for the first 3 years (SM 4(h)).
Specific SEBI time limits and percentages change often; check the current SEBI circular before quoting a number.

Q.q:
Mr. X earns 10% on his investments in equity shares. He is considering a recently floated scheme of a Mutual Fund where the initial expenses are 6% and annual recurring expenses are expected to be 2%.

How much should the Mutual Fund scheme earn to provide a return of 10% to Mr. X?
Q.a:
Formula: r2 = [1 ÷ (1 − Initial expenses)] × r1 + Recurring expenses

Computation: r2 = [1 ÷ (1 − 0.06)] × 0.10 + 0.02 = 0.1064 + 0.02 = 0.1264

Answer: The scheme must earn 12.64% to give Mr. X his 10%.

(Worked example in para 6.2 of the SM.)
Q.trap: Adding the percentages (10% + 6% + 2% = 18%). The initial expense is a one-time loss of capital, so you gross up r1 by dividing by (1 − 0.06); only the recurring expense is added.

Q.q: Explain how to establish a Mutual Fund.
Q.a:
Registration: A mutual fund must be registered with SEBI before it can collect funds from the public. All mutual funds are governed by the same regulations and are subject to SEBI monitoring and inspection.

Sponsor: The fund is established through a sponsor — any body corporate which, alone or with another body corporate, establishes a mutual fund after completing the formalities in SEBI's Mutual Fund Regulations. The sponsor is like a promoter: it provides initial capital and appoints the trustees. It must be in financial services for not less than 5 years, financially sound and a fit party in SEBI's eyes.

Trust: The fund is set up as a trustee company or a Trust under the Indian Trusts Act. The trust deed is executed by the sponsor in favour of the trustees, registered under the Indian Registration Act, 1908, and contains the clauses in the Third Schedule of the Regulations. Trustees hold the fund's property in trust for unit holders.

AMC: An SEBI-approved Asset Management Company manages the fund and operates its schemes. It is a limited company with a minimum net worth of ₹100 crore (as per the SM); the sponsor contributes at least 40% of the net worth.

Independence: At least two-thirds of the directors of the trustee company / board of trustees must be independent of the sponsor; 50% of AMC directors must be independent. The AMC's appointment can be terminated by a majority of trustees or by 75% of unit holders of the scheme.

Fees: The AMC may charge investment management and advisory fees within the ceiling and get scheme operating expenses reimbursed.

Custodian: A SEBI-registered custodian, independent of the sponsor and AMC, holds the securities (through a Depository Participant for demat securities).
Q.trap: Writing only "register with SEBI and form a trust". Marks are for each constituent — sponsor (5 years, 40%), trustees (⅔ independent), AMC (net worth, 50% independent, removal by 75% unit holders) and custodian.

Q.q: What are the advantages of investing in Mutual Funds?
Q.a:
ICAI answer: refer paragraph 4 of the chapter. Write each head with one line:

  • Professional management — skilled managers backed by research analysts.
  • Diversification — many securities, lower concentration risk.
  • Convenient administration — demat, no share-transfer risk or delay.
  • Higher returns over the medium to long term (look at long-run averages, not boom returns).
  • Low cost of management — SEBI cap of 2.5% for equity funds; excess borne by the AMC.
  • Liquidity — repurchase by open-ended funds; listing for close-ended funds.
  • Transparency — portfolio disclosure at least half-yearly; daily NAV published through AMFI.
  • Other benefits — SIP, SWP and switches (ELSS restricts switch-out for 3 years).
  • Highly regulated by SEBI.
  • Economies of scale — pooled money makes investing cheaper and gives retail investors market access.
  • Flexibility — SIP/SWP and a wide range of schemes.
  • Convenience — easy investment and redemption through digital portals.

Q.q: Mr. A can earn a return of 16 per cent by investing in equity shares on his own. Now he is considering a recently announced equity based mutual fund scheme in which initial expenses are 5.5 per cent and annual recurring expenses are 1.5 per cent. How much should the mutual fund earn to provide Mr. A return of 16 per cent?
Q.a:
Personal earnings of Mr. A = R1 = 16%; Mutual Fund earnings = R2

R2 = [1 ÷ (1 − Initial expenses)] × R1 + Recurring expenses

= [1 ÷ (1 − 0.055)] × 16% + 1.5% = 16.93% + 1.5%

Mutual fund must earn 18.43%.
Q.trap: Dividing 16% by (1 − 0.055 − 0.015). Recurring expenses are added after grossing up, not deducted in the denominator.

Q.q:
The unit price of Equity Linked Savings Scheme (ELSS) of a mutual fund is ₹10/-. The public offer price (POP) of the unit is ₹10.204 and the redemption price is ₹9.80.

Calculate: (i) Front-end Load (ii) Back end Load
Q.a:
(i) Front-end load: Public Offer Price = NAV ÷ (1 − Front-end load)

10.204 = 10 ÷ (1 − F) → F = 0.0199, say 2%

(ii) Back-end load: Redemption Price = NAV ÷ (1 + Back-end load)

9.80 = 10 ÷ (1 + B) → B = 0.0204, i.e. 2.04%

Alternative: Front-end load = (10.204 − 10.00) ÷ 10.00 = 0.0204 or 2.04%; Exit load = (10.00 − 9.80) ÷ 10.00 = 0.020 or 2.00%. Both methods are shown in ICAI's answer.

A Mutual Fund having 300 units has shown its NAV of ₹8.75 and ₹9.45 at the beginning and at the end of the year respectively. The Mutual Fund has given two options: (i) Pay ₹0.75 per unit as dividend and ₹0.60 per unit as a capital gain, or (ii) These distributions are to be reinvested at an average NAV of ₹8.65 per unit.

What difference would it make in terms of return available and which option is preferable?

(i) Returns for the year (per unit): change in price ₹9.45 − ₹8.75 = ₹0.70; dividend ₹0.75; capital gains distribution ₹0.60; total ₹2.05

Holding period reward = 2.05 ÷ 8.75 × 100 = 23.43%

(ii) Reinvested at ₹8.65: distribution per unit ₹1.35; total ₹1.35 × 300 = ₹405; additional units = 405 ÷ 8.65 = 46.82; total units 346.82

Value at year end = 346.82 × ₹9.45 = ₹3,277.45; cost = 300 × ₹8.75 = ₹2,625.00; reward = ₹652.45

Holding period reward = 652.45 ÷ 2,625 × 100 = 24.85%

Conclusion: The holding period reward is higher under option (ii), reinvestment of distributions at an average NAV of ₹8.65, so option (ii) is preferable.

Q.q: Identify the type of risks to which the Bond Funds are exposed to. (4 Marks)
Q.a:
Like equity mutual funds, bond funds also have following risks.

- Interest Rate Risk: This risk relates to fluctuation in market value of Bond consequent upon the change in interest rate (YTM) as discussed in the chapter on Security Valuation. There is inverse relationship between market value of bond and interest rate. As interest rate goes up market value of Bond falls and vice versa.

- Credit Risk: This risk is similar to risk of default in repayment of loans or payment of interest or both by the borrowers of the funds. Thus, this risk takes place when a Mutual Fund invested money in the Bonds of a company which defaults in the payment of Interest or Principal. This risk is higher in case of companies with lower Credit Rating.

- Prepayment Risk: This risk is related to early refund of money by the issuer of Bonds before the date of maturity. This generally happens in case of falling interest rates when a company who already issued Bond at higher interest rate issues fresh Bonds at lower rate of interest exercising its right of early redemption of Callable Bonds and refunding the money raised out of fresh issue.

- Reinvestment Risk: In a falling interest rate scenario, on maturity of the Bonds on its due date, the maturity proceeds get invested at a lower rate of interest. This brings down the overall yield of the Portfolio. This is known as a Reinvestment Risk. This turns out to be favourable in a rising interest rate scenario. (4 marks)

Q.q: Explain the various Qualitative factors that need to be taken into account in addition to Quantitative Factors to evaluate the performance of any Mutual Fund. (4 Marks)
Q.a:
Some of the Qualitative factors that need to be taken into account in addition to Quantitative Factors are as follows:

(1) Quality of Portfolio: Quality of stocks and securities in the portfolio of the Mutual Funds is an important qualitative parameter. The reason is that the quality of the portfolio plays a big role in achieving superior returns. The qualitative characteristic of portfolio of Equity Mutual Fund involves allocation of funds in top Blue-chip companies, large companies and how diversified is the portfolio. The style followed can be growth, value or blend of the same. In Debt Funds, the quality of portfolio is measured on the basis of credit quality, average maturity and modified duration of the fixed asset securities.

Not only that it is necessary that Mutual Fund should hold good quality stocks or securities, but it is also necessary the investment should be as per the objective of the Fund. Under normal circumstances, the fund having lower Portfolio Turnover ratio is considered to be better.

(2) Track record and competence of Fund Manager: Since Fund Manager decides about the selection of securities and takes investment decisions, his/her competence and conviction plays a very big role. The competence of a Fund Manager is assessed from his/her knowledge and ability to manage in addition to past performance.

(3) Credibility of Fund House Team: Team of Fund House also plays a big role towards the investors' interest. In addition to investment decisions, there are some other administrative tasks also such as redemption of units, crediting of dividend, providing adequate information etc. which play a crucial role in qualitative assessment of any mutual fund house.
Q.trap: Writing Sharpe/Treynor (quantitative). The question wants the three qualitative factors.

Q.q: EXPLAIN how to measure divergence or deviation of return of a Mutual Fund Scheme that replicates any benchmark Index. (4 Marks)
Q.a:
Tracking error can be used to measure the divergence or deviation of a fund's return from the benchmarks return it is following.

The passive fund managers closely follow or track the benchmark index. Although they design their investment strategy on the same index but often it may not exactly replicate the index return. In such situation, there is possibility of deviation between the returns.

The tracking error can be calculated on the basis of corresponding benchmark return vis a vis quarterly or monthly average NAVs.

Higher the tracking error higher is the risk profile of the fund. Whether the funds outperform or underperform their benchmark indices; it clearly indicates that of fund managers are not following the benchmark indices properly. In addition to the same other reason for tracking error are as follows:

- Transaction cost

- Fees charged by AMCs

- Fund expenses

- Cash holdings

- Sampling biasness

Thus, from above it can be said that to replicate the return to any benchmark index the tracking error should be near to zero.

The Tracking Error is calculated as follows: TE = √[Σ(d – d̄)² / (n – 1)], where d = Differential return; d̄ = Average differential return; n = No. of observation. Total Marks = 4

Q.q: Explain the different methods for evaluating the performance of a mutual fund. (4 Marks)
Q.a:
Note: ICAI's answer file for this MTP prints an answer to a different question, so there is no ICAI solution. This answer is written from SM para 7 (Evaluation of Mutual Funds).

Quantitative parameters

  • Risk-adjusted returns: of two funds with the same return, prefer the one with lower risk.
  • Benchmark returns: a good fund beats its benchmark in all phases; the excess is alpha.
  • Comparison with peers in the same category.
  • Returns across economic and market cycles, not one short period.
  • Financial measures: expense ratio; Sharpe ratio (return over total risk); Treynor ratio (return over β); Sortino ratio (return over downside deviation).

Qualitative parameters

  • Quality of portfolio: blue chips, diversification, style; credit quality, maturity and modified duration for debt funds; low portfolio turnover.
  • Track record and competence of the fund manager.
  • Credibility of the fund house team: redemptions, dividend credits, information to investors.

Evaluate at least every 6–12 months, giving an equity fund 3–5 years, because past performance does not guarantee future performance.
Q.trap: Only listing ratios. Marks are also given for benchmark, peers, cycles and the qualitative factors.

Q.q:
Index Funds is one of the Special Funds. What are other funds in Special Funds category? (4 Marks)

(This is the OR alternative to a commodity-characteristic-approach question.)
Q.a:
The other funds in Special Fund category are as follows:

(a) International Funds: A mutual fund located in India to raise money in India for investing globally.

(b) Offshore Funds: A mutual fund located in India to raise money globally for investing in India.

(c) Sector Funds: They invest their entire fund in a particular industry e.g. utility fund for utility industry like power, gas, public works.

(d) Money Market Funds: These are predominantly debt-oriented schemes, whose main objective is preservation of capital, easy liquidity and moderate income. To achieve this objective, liquid funds invest predominantly in safer short-term instruments like Commercial Papers, Certificate of Deposits, Treasury Bills, G-Secs etc.

(e) Fund of Funds: Fund of Funds (FoF) as the name suggests are schemes which invest in other mutual fund schemes. The concept is popular in markets where there are number of mutual fund offerings and choosing a suitable scheme according to one's objective is tough. Just as a mutual fund scheme invests in a portfolio of securities such as equity, debt etc., the underlying investments for a FoF is the units of other mutual fund schemes, either from the same fund family or from other fund houses.

(f) Capital Protection Oriented Fund: The term 'capital protection oriented scheme' means a mutual fund scheme which is designated as such and which endeavours to protect the capital invested therein through suitable orientation of its portfolio structure. The orientation towards protection of capital originates from the portfolio structure of the scheme and not from any bank guarantee, insurance cover etc.

(g) Gold Funds: The objective of these funds is to track the performance of Gold. The units represent the value of gold or gold related instruments held in the scheme. Gold Funds which are generally in the form of an Exchange Traded Fund (ETF) are listed on the stock exchange and offers investors an opportunity to participate in the bullion market without having to take physical delivery of gold.

(h) Quant Funds: Quant Fund works on a data-driven approach for stock selection and investment decisions based on a pre-determined rules or parameters using statistics or mathematics-based models.
Q.trap: Listing equity or debt fund types (growth, income, gilt). The question asks for the special funds category of para 2.2.3.

Q.a:
(a) ELSS — deduction under s.80C; 3-year lock-in; risk: equity market risk, and money is locked for 3 years.

(b) Fixed Maturity Plan — investments mature with the fund, so it is free from interest rate risk if held to maturity; risk: credit risk (default/downgrade, especially in AA and lower paper used to boost yield) and illiquidity (listed but thinly traded).

(c) Multicap fund — at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps; risk: the mandatory small/mid-cap exposure is more volatile. (A flexicap fund has no fixed minimum.)
Q.trap: Suggesting a gilt fund for (b). Gilt funds have no credit risk but do carry interest rate risk; the FMP is the one designed to avoid it.

Q.q: An equity fund returned 14% over three years against 11% for its benchmark. Mr. Q, who invested in the same fund, lost money. Explain, with reference to the drawbacks of mutual funds, how this can happen and what he should look at before choosing a fund.
Q.a:
Entry and exit points: a fund may beat the market, but each investor's return depends on when he entered and left (SM 5(a)(ii)). If Mr. Q bought near a peak and sold in a fall, he can lose despite the fund's 3-year record.

No guarantee of return: in a sharp fall (2008, Covid-19 2020) principal can be lost in the short term; over longer periods the chance is remote (5(a)(iii)).

Cost factor: exit load if he redeemed early, and recurring expenses not linked to performance (5(d)).

Selection: past performance is the main criterion but cannot predict the future (5(c)).

Before choosing: evaluate risk-adjusted return, benchmark and peers, returns across market cycles, expense ratio, and qualitative factors (portfolio quality, fund manager, fund house) — and invest through a SIP to average the entry price.

Q.q: How can Foreign Institutional Investors invest in Indian mutual funds, and how does their participation benefit the Indian economy?
Q.a:
Route: FIIs may buy units of domestic mutual funds directly from the issuer or through a registered stock broker on a recognised stock exchange, within the limits notified by SEBI.

Benefits: (a) Enhanced corporate governance — FIIs carry out thorough due diligence before investing; (b) Improved competition in the capital market; (c) Improved inflow of capital — employment is generated and the foreign exchange position improves.

Caution: FIIs often fuel a bullish market for a short period, so inflows can reverse.

Q.q: Ms. R can save ₹5,000 a month. She has no time to study companies but wants equity exposure. Should she buy shares directly or invest through a mutual fund? Advise.
Q.a:
Diversification: a well-diversified portfolio needs 15–20 stocks; ₹5,000 a month cannot buy that directly, but a fund gives a wide basket for ₹5,000.

Cost: brokerage on small purchases eats into returns; pooled money gives economies of scale.

Time and skill: stock picking needs constant research and monitoring; she has neither time nor inclination.

Discipline: a SIP of ₹5,000 a month invests automatically and averages her cost (more units when NAV is low).

Advice: invest through a diversified equity fund by SIP, preferably the direct plan; review every 6–12 months.

(iv) Without a side pocket, the bond would be written down in the main NAV; investors who enter later at that low NAV would share any recovery they did not suffer, and those who rush to redeem force distress selling. Q.q: A finance company with 3 years in financial services, profitable throughout, wants to sponsor a mutual fund. It proposes to own 100% of the AMC, appoint its own directors as all the trustees, and keep the securities in its own custody. Comment.
Q.a:
Sponsor eligibility: SEBI requires the sponsor to be in financial services for not less than 5 years; 3 years does not qualify.

AMC ownership: the sponsor must contribute at least 40% of the AMC's net worth — owning 100% is permitted, but the AMC board must have at least 50% independent directors.

Trustees: at least two-thirds must be independent of the sponsor; appointing only its own directors breaches this.

Custody: securities must be held by a SEBI-registered custodian independent of the sponsor and the AMC.

Conclusion: the proposal fails on sponsor experience, trustee independence and custody, and needs independent AMC directors.
Q.trap: Accepting it because the company is profitable. Track record (5 years) is a separate condition.

method: Lay out units, NAVs and cash flows in a table before any formula: units = amount ÷ NAV; dividends on face value; reinvested units at ex-dividend NAV; bonus units by ratio. Label every column with units (₹, ₹ lakh, units).

Write the formula in symbols first (NAV = net assets ÷ units; r = (NAV<sub>1</sub> − NAV<sub>0</sub> + I + G) ÷ NAV<sub>0</sub>). Examiners give a mark for the right formula even if the arithmetic slips.

Bold the final figure with ₹ or %. If the question asks 'which option is better' or 'comment', end with one sentence of advice (e.g. 'Reinvestment gives 24.85% against 23.43%; option (ii) is preferable').
Use the SM's headings as points (e.g. the 12 advantages, the 4 fund-manager roles, sponsor–trust–AMC–custodian). One line of explanation per point; 4–6 points for 4 marks.

Keep 4 decimals in NAV until the last step (ICAI uses ₹78.8366 to issue units). Show the alternative method where ICAI gives one (load % two ways; simple yield vs IRR). Count days exactly for effective yield.
