formulas.title: NAV: what one unit is worth
formulas.idea: Everything in this chapter starts with NAV. A mutual fund is a big shared basket; NAV is the value of one slice of that basket.

master.name: NAV per unit
master.logic:
Imagine a pizza worth ₹800 shared by 8 friends. Each slice is worth ₹100. The fund is the pizza, the units are the slices, NAV is the value of one slice.

If the fund owes money (expenses, payables), that is taken out of the pizza first — friends only share what is left.
vars: Everything the fund owns at market value minus everything it owes
Units in issue on that date (after any new issue / repurchase)
master.hook: Slice value = what is left ÷ number of slices.
master.cue: "Calculate NAV", "NAV per unit", a list of shares × prices and a number of units.
master.trap: Using face value (₹10) instead of the units outstanding, or forgetting accrued expenses and other liabilities.
master.example: Shares worth ₹4,20,20,000, accrued expenses ₹2,50,000, other liabilities ₹2,00,000, 10 lakh units → (4,20,20,000 − 4,50,000) ÷ 10,00,000 = ₹41.57 (SM TYK).

items.name: Net assets
items.expr: Net assets = MV of investments + Receivables + Accrued income + Other assets − Accrued expenses − Payables − Other liabilities
items.logic: List what the fund owns (at today's market value), then subtract what it owes. Same as a household: bank balance + things you own − bills not yet paid.
items.derive: This is the numerator of the master NAV formula.
items.trap: Valuing shares at cost. Use market value; listed bonds at their NAV-date value; unlisted bonds at cost less any diminution.

items.name: Units issued to a new investor
items.expr: New units = Amount investedNAV on that day
items.logic: A new friend joins and pays for slices at today's slice price. If each slice costs ₹78.84 and he pays ₹30 lakh, he gets 30,00,000 ÷ 78.84 slices. Nobody else's slice changes in value — that is why funds issue units at NAV.
items.derive: Rearranged NAV: units = value ÷ NAV per unit.
items.cue: "Mr. A submits a cheque of ₹…", "HNI sends a cheque".
items.trap: Rounding NAV before dividing. ICAI divides by the unrounded NAV (₹78.8366) to get 6,38,053 units.

items.name: Shares valued by index movement
items.expr: Value today = Cost × Index todayIndex at purchase
items.logic: If you bought the whole market when the index was 1,000 and the index is now 2,300, your shares have grown in the same proportion: 2.3 times.
items.example: ₹20 crore × 2,300 ÷ 1,000 = ₹46 crore (SM TYK regular income scheme).
items.cue: "Listed shares were purchased when index was …; present index is …".

items.name: NAV after a dividend
items.expr: NAV<sub>ex</sub> = NAV<sub>cum</sub> − Dividend per unit
items.logic: When the fund pays out cash, that cash leaves the basket. So every slice becomes lighter by exactly the amount paid out.
items.derive: Net assets fall by (DPS × units); divide by the same units → NAV falls by DPS.

formulas.title: Entry and exit loads: the price you pay and get
formulas.idea: A load is a toll. On the way in you pay a bit more than NAV; on the way out you get a bit less. All load formulas are NAV with the toll added or removed.

master.name: Dealing price = NAV ± load
master.expr: Buy price = NAV + entry toll · Sell price = NAV − exit toll
master.logic: Think of a toll road: going in costs a little extra, coming out you lose a little. The fund itself is still worth NAV.

items.name: Public offer price (front-end load)
items.expr: POP = NAV1 − f
items.logic: ICAI's version treats the load as a slice of the price you pay: of every ₹100 you pay, f% is the toll and the rest buys NAV. So NAV = POP × (1 − f).
items.trap: ICAI accepts the alternative load = (POP − NAV) ÷ NAV = 2.04% too — show both if time allows.

items.name: Redemption price (back-end load)
items.expr: Redemption price = NAV1 + b
items.logic: On the way out, the toll is charged on top of the price you receive, so NAV = Redemption price × (1 + b).

items.name: Load as a % of NAV (alternative)
items.expr: Entry load = POP − NAVNAV · Exit load = NAV − Redemption priceNAV
items.logic: Simplest view: how much more (or less) than NAV, as a share of NAV. This is also how ICAI prices issues in dividend-equalisation sums: NAV × (1 + 2%).

items.name: Real return
items.expr: Real return = 1 + Nominal return1 + Inflation − 1
items.logic: If your money grew 27.71% but prices grew 4.5%, you can buy only 1.2771 ÷ 1.045 = 1.2221 times as much stuff — 22.21% more, not 23.21%.
items.trap: Subtracting inflation (27.71 − 4.50) — that is only an approximation.

formulas.title: Return a fund must earn (covering costs)
formulas.idea: A fund has two kinds of cost: a one-time initial expense (eats part of your capital on day 1) and a yearly recurring expense. The fund must earn enough to cover both and still give you what you could earn alone.

master.name: Required return of the scheme
master.logic: You give ₹100. Initial expense of 6% means only ₹94 actually gets invested. To give you ₹10 (10% of your ₹100), the ₹94 must earn 10 ÷ 94 = 10.64%. Then the fund also takes 2% every year, so it must earn 2% more: 12.64%.
vars: return the investor earns on his own
master.hook: Gross up for the one-time cost, add on the yearly cost.
master.cue: "How much should the mutual fund earn to provide Mr. A a return of x%?"
master.trap: Adding all three (10 + 6 + 2 = 18%) or dividing the recurring expense too.

items.name: What the investor actually gets
items.expr: r1 = (r2 − Recurring exp.) × (1 − Initial exp.)
items.logic: Run the same story backwards: take away the yearly cost from what the fund earns, then remember only (1 − initial) of your money was working.

formulas.title: Returns: how much did the investor make?
formulas.idea: Every return formula in this chapter is one idea: (what you have at the end − what you put in + what you were paid along the way) ÷ what you put in. The rest only change the time scale (month, year, days) or how "paid along the way" is handled (cash or reinvested).

master.name: Holding period return (the master)
master.expr: Return = End value − Start value + Cash receivedStart value
master.logic: You planted a ₹100 tree. A year later it is worth ₹110 and you also picked ₹5 of fruit. You gained ₹15 on ₹100 = 15%.

items.name: Return per unit with distributions
items.expr: r = (NAVt − NAVt−1) + It + GtNAVt−1
items.logic: The master formula for one unit: change in NAV + income paid + capital gain paid, over the starting NAV.
items.cue: "made income and capital gain distribution of ₹… per unit", "calculate return".

items.name: Closing NAV from a known return
items.expr: NAVt = NAVt−1 × (1 + r) − I − G
items.logic: If you know how much the fund returned, the NAV at the end is what the start grew to, minus whatever was paid out (paid-out money is no longer inside the NAV).
items.trap: Using 15% for a month. Convert the annual return to monthly first (15% ÷ 12).

items.name: Return when distributions are reinvested
items.expr: Return = (Units0 + Distributions ÷ NAVre) × NAVend − CostCost
items.logic: Instead of taking the fruit, you plant it — it buys more units at the reinvestment NAV. At the end you count all units at the closing NAV.
items.derive: Master formula with "cash received" = 0 and the end value including the extra units.
items.cue: "distributions are reinvested at an average NAV of ₹…", "which option is preferable".
items.trap: If the reinvestment NAV is below the closing NAV, reinvesting wins (extra units bought cheap). Always end with a one-line recommendation.

items.name: Effective yield per annum
items.expr: Yield p.a. = (Units × NAVend − Investment) + DividendsInvestment × 365Days held
items.logic: First find the return for the time you actually held it (master formula), then stretch it to a full year: if you made 1% in 36.5 days, a year has 10 such periods.
items.derive: Holding period return × (365 ÷ days). Simple annualisation, not compounding.
items.trap: Counting months instead of days, or miscounting days. Count actual days in each month.

items.name: Days held (reverse)
items.expr: Days = Holding period yield % × 365Effective yield p.a. %
items.logic: Reverse the stretch: if the yearly figure is 9.66% and you actually made 2.5146%, you held it for 2.5146 ÷ 9.66 of a year.
items.cue: "has misplaced the documents… find the date of investment".

items.name: Annualised yield → yield for the period
items.expr: Period yield = Annualised yield × Months held12
items.logic: ICAI's "annualised yield" in Mr X sums is simple: 153.33% a year for 9 months is 115%.
items.trap: If the question says "holding period return" (SM TYK 13, PYQ Nov 2024), do NOT scale — it already is the period figure.

items.name: Monthly ↔ annual return (simple)
items.expr: rannual = rmonthly × 12 · Annual return = Net gainInvestment × 12Months
items.logic: ICAI annualises MF returns simply (no compounding) unless it asks for IRR or geometric mean.
items.example: ABC MF: 1% a month → 12% p.a. Sun Moon: gain ₹6,98,969.69 on ₹1,00,000 over 124 months → 67.64% p.a.

items.name: Geometric (compound) return per period
items.expr: rGM = (End valueStart value)1/n − 1
items.logic: If something doubles in 3 years, it did not grow 33.3% a year — it grew by the number that, multiplied by itself 3 times, gives 2. That is the n-th root.
items.example: Closed-end fund price ₹20 → ₹23.192 over 4 periods: (1.1596)1/4 − 1 = 3.771%; NAV 20 → 22.3: 2.76% (PYQ May 2026).
items.trap: Dividing the total return by n (15.96% ÷ 4 = 3.99%) is the arithmetic average, not the geometric one asked.

items.name: Market price of a closed-ended unit
items.expr: Price = NAV × (1 + premium %) or NAV × (1 − discount %)
items.logic: Close-ended units trade on the exchange like shares, so buyers may pay more (premium) or less (discount) than the slice is really worth.

items.name: IRR by interpolation (ICAI's alternative for plan yields)
items.expr: IRR = LR + NPV at LRNPV at LR − NPV at HR × (HR − LR)
items.logic: Try two rates: one gives a positive NPV, one negative. The true rate sits between them, proportionally closer to the one with the smaller NPV.

formulas.title: Units trail: dividend reinvestment and bonus plans
formulas.idea: Plan sums are just bookkeeping of how many units you hold. Every event adds units; at the end, units × NAV is your money. Going backwards (to find an issue price) you undo each event in reverse order.

master.name: New units = cash to reinvest ÷ price
master.expr: New units = Cash to reinvestPrice per unit
master.logic: Same as buying anything: ₹100 at ₹20 each buys 5. Every units formula below is this one.

items.name: Units from dividend reinvestment
items.expr: New units = Units held × Face value × Dividend %Ex-dividend NAV
items.logic: Dividend is declared as a % of the face value (₹10), not NAV. That cash buys units at the NAV after the dividend.
items.derive: Cash to reinvest = units × ₹10 × d%; price = ex-dividend NAV.
items.trap: Taking the dividend % on NAV. A "20% dividend" on a ₹10 unit is ₹2 a unit.

items.name: Units from a bonus issue
items.expr: Bonus units = Units held × ab (for an a : b bonus)
items.logic: "1:5" means 1 free unit for every 5 you hold. No cash moves, so it is units × 1/5. NAV drops to share the same value over more units.

items.name: Undoing a reinvestment (backwards)
items.expr: Units before = Units after1 + Face value × d% ÷ NAV = Units after × NAVNAV + Dividend per unit
items.logic: After the event you hold N + N × (div ÷ NAV) units. Divide out that growth factor to get N back.
items.derive: N + N × D ÷ NAV = Units after → N = Units after ÷ (1 + D/NAV) = Units after × NAV ÷ (NAV + D).
items.example: 43,120 after a 30% dividend at NAV 45: N/15 + N = 43,120 → N = 40,425 (PYQ Dec 2021 old).
items.trap: Subtracting dividend ÷ NAV of the closing units — the new units were bought on the old units only.

items.name: Undoing a bonus (backwards)
items.expr: Units before = Units after × ba + b
items.logic: After a 2:5 bonus, every 5 units became 7. So the "before" is 5/7 of "after".

items.name: Issue price from average yield or profit
items.expr: Issue price = InvestmentOriginal units, where Original units come from Investment + Avg gain × YearsClosing NAV undone event by event
items.logic: Rebuild the end: what you invested + all the gains = what you have now. Divide by today's NAV to know today's units, peel off the bonus/reinvested units in reverse, and you know how many you first bought.
items.cue: "details (except the issue price) are available", "Average Profit", "Average Yield".

items.name: Value and return of a plan
items.expr: Value = Final units × Final NAV (− STT − tax) · Return p.a. = Value − InvestmentInvestment × 12Months
items.logic: After the units trail, it is the master return formula again.
items.trap: Short-term capital gains tax only on units bought in the last 12 months (the latest reinvested or bonus units).

formulas.title: Performance: reward per unit of risk
formulas.idea: Every evaluation ratio is extra return ÷ some measure of risk. "Extra return" is what the fund earned above a risk-free bank deposit (Rp − Rf). The ratios differ only in which risk goes underneath. Because they share the same top, you can divide one by another to find β — that is the trick ICAI keeps testing.

master.name: Reward-to-risk (the master)
master.logic: Two runners finish 1 km. One ran on flat ground, one up a hill. The hill runner deserves more credit. Return is the distance; risk is the hill.

items.name: Sharpe ratio (total risk)
items.expr: Sharpe = Rp − Rfσp
items.logic: Uses σ — all the ups and downs of the fund. Right for an investor who holds only this fund, so all its wobble matters.

items.name: Treynor ratio (market risk)
items.expr: Treynor = Rp − Rfβp
items.logic: Uses β — only the wobble that comes from the market. Right for a well-diversified investor, whose other holdings already cancel the fund-specific wobble.

items.name: Sortino ratio (downside risk)
items.expr: Sortino = Rp − RfDownside deviation
items.logic: Investors do not mind surprises upward. Sortino counts only the bad wobble — returns below the target.

items.name: β from Sharpe and Treynor
items.expr: β = Sharpe × σTreynor
items.logic: Sharpe × σ gives back the extra return (Rp − Rf). Divide that extra return by Treynor and you get β, because Treynor = extra return ÷ β.
items.derive: Sharpe = E ÷ σ → E = Sharpe × σ. Treynor = E ÷ β → β = E ÷ Treynor = Sharpe × σ ÷ Treynor.
items.cue: Sharpe, Treynor and σ given together; "expected NAV if the market falls x%".

items.name: β from correlation
items.expr: βp = ρpm × σpσm = Cov(p, m)σm2
items.logic: β asks: when the market moves 1%, how much does the fund move? It depends on how much the fund wobbles (σp), compared with the market's wobble (σm), and how much of the wobble is in step with the market (ρ).
items.derive: Cov = ρ σp σm; β = Cov ÷ σm2 = ρ σp ÷ σm.
items.trap: "Variance of the market is 9" means σm = 3, not 9 (PYQ Nov 2022).

items.name: Correlation and coefficient of determination
items.expr: ρ = β × σmσp · R2 = ρ2
items.logic: R² tells you what share of the fund's wobble is explained by the market. ρ = 0.53 → R² = 0.28: only 28% of its moves come from the market.
items.example: Growth fund: β 0.75, σ 10, σm 7.1 → ρ 0.5325 → R² 0.2836 (PYQ Nov 2024).

items.name: σ from Sharpe
items.expr: σp = Rp − RfSharpe · Variance = σ2
items.logic: Rearrange Sharpe. Negative Sharpe (fund below risk-free) still gives a positive σ because both top and bottom are negative.

items.name: CAPM expected return
items.expr: E(R<sub>p</sub>) = R<sub>f</sub> + β (R<sub>m</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>)
items.logic: A fund should earn the bank rate plus a reward for the market risk it takes: β times the market's extra return.

items.name: Jensen's alpha
items.expr: α = R<sub>p</sub> − [R<sub>f</sub> + β (R<sub>m</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>)]
items.logic: Actual return minus what CAPM says it should have earned for its β. Positive α = the manager added value.
items.example: Smart MF: 8.50% − 1.10% α = 7.40% expected; with Treynor solve β 0.35, Rf 6% (PYQ May 2023).

items.name: Risk per unit of return
items.expr: Risk per unit of return = σExpected return
items.logic: The upside-down of a reward ratio: how much wobble you accept for each 1% of return. Lower is better.

items.name: M² (Modigliani) measure
items.expr: M<sup>2</sup> = R<sub>f</sub> + Sharpe<sub>p</sub> × σ<sub>m</sub> (compare with R<sub>m</sub>)
items.logic: Pretend the fund were mixed with risk-free money so its σ equals the market's. What return would it then earn? If more than the market, it beat the market on a fair, same-risk basis.

items.name: Information ratio
items.expr: IR = Rp − RbTracking error
items.logic: Like Sharpe, but against the benchmark instead of the bank: extra return over the index ÷ how far the fund strays from the index.

items.name: Expected NAV after a market move
items.expr: NAV<sub>new</sub> = Equity × (1 + β × Market change) + (Cash − Expenses for the period)
items.logic: Only the shares move with the market (by β times the market move). Cash just sits there, minus the month's running costs.
items.trap: Applying β to the cash part, or forgetting the period's expenses.

formulas.title: Tracking error: how faithfully an index fund copies its index
formulas.idea: An index fund promises to copy the index. Each period, note the gap between the fund and the index. Tracking error is how much those gaps wobble — a standard deviation of the gaps.

master.name: Tracking error
master.logic: If the fund is always exactly 0.5% behind, the gap never wobbles and TE is zero (it is a cost drag, not tracking error). TE grows when the gap jumps around.
vars: differential return each period = R<sub>fund</sub> − R<sub>index</sub>
master.trap: Dividing by n instead of n − 1, or using the raw returns instead of the differences.
master.cue: "fund return vs benchmark return over several periods", "passive fund".

items.name: Differential return
items.expr: d = Rfund − Rbenchmark · d̄ = Σ dn
items.logic: Step 1 of TE: subtract index return from fund return every period, then average them.

formulas.title: Fund accounts: cash, net assets and the investor's rate of earning
formulas.idea: For a new fund over a month or a year, follow the cash like a bank statement, then add the portfolio at market value and deduct what is still owed. That gives net assets → NAV → the investor's earning.

master.name: Closing net assets
master.expr: Closing net assets = Closing cash + Portfolio at market + Receivables − Outstanding liabilities
master.logic: Money in the bank + what the shares are worth + money still to come in − bills still to pay.

items.name: Opening cash
items.expr: Opening cash = Money raised − Initial expenses (or underwriting, marketing) − Portfolio bought
items.logic: Whatever was raised and not spent or invested on day 1 is in the bank.

items.name: Closing cash
items.expr: Closing cash = Opening cash + Sale proceeds + Dividends/interest received − Purchases − Expenses paid − Distributions
items.logic: A bank statement: add what came in, subtract what went out.
items.trap: Only expenses actually paid leave the bank; arrears are a liability deducted from net assets later.

items.name: Distribution of realised earnings
items.expr: Distribution = Payout % × (Realised capital gains + Dividends/interest)
items.logic: Funds pay out from profits that are "real" — securities actually sold and dividends earned — not from paper gains on shares still held.

items.name: Chargeable management expense
items.expr: Chargeable = Lower of (Actual, Cap % × Average funds invested) · Average = Opening + Closing investment2
items.logic: A regulator's cap is a ceiling: you can charge what you spent, but never more than the cap.

items.name: Investor's rate of earning
items.expr: Earning per unit = Distributions per unit + (Closing NAV − Issue price) · Rate = Earning per unitIssue price
items.logic: The investor got some cash along the way and then sold at closing NAV — the master return formula for one unit.

formulas.title: Dividend equalisation: new units buy their share of income already earned
formulas.idea: If a fund has earned ₹0.08 a unit of undistributed income and a new investor joins, he would share in income he did not help earn. So he pays that ₹0.08 on top of the price; someone leaving gets it back. Income per unit stays equal for everyone.

master.name: Income per unit
master.expr: Income per unit = Undistributed income so farUnits outstanding
master.logic: The pot of income earned but not yet paid, shared per unit.

items.name: Issue price with equalisation
items.expr: Issue price = Opening NAV × (1 + entry load) + Income per unit to date
items.logic: Price of the slice + toll + your share of income already in the pot.

items.name: Repurchase price with equalisation
items.expr: Repurchase price = Opening NAV × (1 − exit load) + Income per unit to date
items.logic: The leaver takes back his share of the income pot.

items.name: Closing NAV in an equalisation sum
items.expr: Closing NAV = Opening net assets + Appreciation + Issue proceeds + Income − Repurchase paid − DividendClosing units
items.logic: Start with the basket, add what grew and came in, subtract what went out, divide by the slices now.

formulas.title: Hedge fund fees: fixed + incentive above the high-water mark
formulas.idea: The manager gets a small fixed fee always, and a bonus only when the fund climbs above its best-ever value (the high-water mark). He cannot earn a bonus twice for recovering the same lost ground.

master.name: Total fee
master.expr: Fee = Fixed % × Assets + Incentive % × max(0, New value − High-water mark)
master.logic: Like a football coach: a salary every season, and a bonus only for beating the club's best-ever season.
master.trap: Paying the incentive on the year's gain over ₹20 crore. Compare with the ₹21 crore high-water mark.

items.name: New fund value
items.expr: New value = Assets × (1 + Return)
items.logic: Grow the opening assets by the year's return.

formulas.title: Constant ratio plan: keep the mix fixed
formulas.idea: You decide, say, 50% shares and 50% bonds. When shares jump, they become more than half — sell some. When they crash, buy some. You automatically sell high and buy low.

master.name: Target value of each side
master.expr: Target equity = Total value × Equity ratio · Total = Bonds + Units × NAV
master.logic: Add up both pots, then split the total back to the chosen ratio.

items.name: Trigger test
items.expr: Rebalance if NAVt − NAVt−1NAVt−1 ≥ +15% or ≤ −15%
items.logic: ICAI compares each month with the previous month (PYQ Nov 2022 says so expressly).

items.name: Units to buy or sell
items.expr: Units to trade = Target equity − Units × NAVNAV
items.logic: Positive → buy that many units; negative → sell.

formulas.title: Gilt fund: NAV and duration management
formulas.idea: Bond prices move opposite to interest rates, and longer-duration bonds move more. So before rates fall you lengthen duration (to gain more); before rates rise you shorten it (to lose less).

master.name: Average duration (simple)
master.expr: Average duration = Σ DurationsNumber of bonds
master.logic: ICAI uses a simple average when told to.

items.name: Revised average duration after a switch
items.expr: Revised = Σ D − Dsold + Dboughtn
items.logic: Take one bond out, put another in, re-average.

items.name: Gilt fund NAV
items.expr: NAV = Σ (Face value × Price ÷ 100)Units
items.logic: Each bond is worth face value × its price per ₹100.

formulas.title: Beyond the study material: concept formulas
formulas.idea: Not in the SM, but they follow from the same ideas and suit concept-based questions. Each is marked Beyond SM.

master.name: SIP: average cost per unit (rupee-cost averaging)
master.expr: Average cost = Total amount investedTotal units bought = harmonic mean of the prices
master.logic: Investing the same ₹ every month buys more units when prices are low and fewer when high. So your average cost per unit is the harmonic mean of the prices, which is always ≤ the simple average price.

items.name: Expense ratio charged daily
items.expr: Daily expense = Net assets × TER365 · TER = Total expensesAverage net assets
items.logic: TER is a yearly %, but NAV is struck daily, so 1/365 of it is deducted from net assets every day.

items.name: NAV with a side pocket (segregated portfolio)
items.expr: Main NAV = Net assets − Stressed assetUnits · Side-pocket NAV = Recoverable value of stressed assetUnits (same count)
items.logic: The bad bond is cut out into its own pot. Every holder keeps the same number of units in both pots: the main pot's NAV shows only the healthy assets; the side pot pays out if and when the bad bond recovers.
items.example: ₹100 crore with a ₹5 crore defaulted bond, 10 crore units → main NAV ₹9.50; side pocket valued at what is expected to be recovered.

items.name: Cost drag over time
items.expr: Final value = Investment × (1 + r − TER)n
items.logic: A 1% yearly cost compounds: over 20 years at 12%, (1.11)20 = 8.06 vs (1.12)20 = 9.65 — about 16% less money. That is why direct plans matter.
